newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-FOCUS-Australian rates are on hold - RBA.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-FOCUS-Australian rates are on hold - RBA.

text.p: An upbeat outlook on the ecomomy by the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) on Tuesday put paid to market speculation of a cut in interest rates anytime soon.
The RBA said it expected the areas of most concern in 1996, such as employment, retail spending and housing, were improving while the main threat to inflation continued to be wages growth.
Inflation was seen well controlled, with the key underlying rate remaining close to two percent in 1997 and staying in the two to three percent target band in 1998.

"Given this assessment of the outlook for inflation and growth, and the uncertainties still surrounding wage outcomes, the Bank sees current monetary policy settings as broadly appropriate for the time being," the RBA said in its quarterly report on the economy, contained in its February Bulletin.
"Information becoming available recently points to a somewhat stronger tone in economic activity than appeared to be the case for much of 1996," the RBA said.
Economists said it appeared that a rate cut would now require an economy weaker than the RBA was expecting.

"It may remain a slim possibility, but there is very little in today's Reserve Bank quarterly report on the economy to suggest grounds for another rate cut," Societe Generale economists said in a commentary.
The RBA's outlook included improvements in three areas of concern in 1996 - employment, the retail and housing sectors.
"Although monthly numbers are extremely volatile, underlying employment growth appears to have picked up," the RBA said.
Retailing conditions appear to have picked up in 1997 after a weak finish to 1996, and should benefit from an expected strengthening in consumption through 1997, the bank said.

It said there was also accumulating evidence that housing was in the early stages of an upturn, and it said the sector should also benefit from the favourable conditions of low interest rates and low rental vacancy rates.
A solid upswing in business investment was underway, and positive outlook "reflects relatively optimistic expectations regarding the medium term future of the Australian economy."
Current interest rates were also favourable for investment, with 'real' rates only slightly above their levels of 1993, when policy was set to stimulate a weak economy, the RBA said.
While the outlook for growth was upbeat, there also little concern on the outlook for inflation.
"In the near term, the bank expects the recent good performance on inflation to be maintained ... the bank expects inflation to be in the two to three percent range in 1998."
"The main uncertainty to the outlook for inflation, and for employment, remains labour costs," the RBA said.

The bank reiterated its earlier warning that the union movement's "living wage" claim would lead to a substantial rise in wages growth, and would almost certainly harm job prospects for the unskilled.
Economists said that given that inflation and growth outlook, and the RBA's assessment of current policy settings, rates may be unchanged for much of 1997.

"We believe that data will point increasingly to strengthening economic activity and the central bank will leave official rates unchanged for the remainder of 1997," Westpac senior economist John Peters said.
The extended period of low inflation and strong growth was also requiring some adjustment to the thinking of the markets.

"We're not used to such a long period of strong growth low inflation, so that's why everyone's a bit nervous, looking for this bogey-man that hasn't come around the corner yet," Citibank chief economist Stephen Koukoulas said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
